A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same min-p sampling method and share identifiable experiments, implementation code and figures. Their main text and appendices are readable and support comparison despite extensive reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original Mistral 7B experiments on GPQA and GSM8K across sampling parameters and temperatures, including results in Figures 2–5.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark experiments, a GSM8K accuracy–diversity analysis, larger-model evaluations and a human study with 54 retained responses.

M1.justification: The threshold pbase × pmax, token filtering and renormalized sampling remain equivalent. The MinPLogitsWarper implementation in v1 Appendix A is retained in v2 Appendix B. Self-consistency is introduced as an evaluation procedure without changing the min-p algorithm.

E1.justification: GPQA, GSM8K and AlpacaEval Creative Writing remain the benchmark coverage. v2 adds a small creative-story study using the prompt 'Write me a creative story?' and English-fluent regular LLM users. Larger models and self-consistency extend evaluation settings rather than benchmark domains.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds top-k, eta and epsilon sampling to the GPQA/GSM8K comparisons, which previously evaluated min-p against top-p and unrestricted sampling. Table 3b also adds epsilon sampling to the creative-writing comparison. Mirostat was already evaluated in v1 Table 3.

E3.justification: v2 adds Mistral Large 123B evaluations, GSM8K self-consistency with an embedding-based entropy measure, and a Llama 3 70B human-study protocol using three outputs per configuration and 1–10 ratings. It also reports additional temperature settings. The existing 5-shot GPQA and 8-shot GSM8K prompting are retained.

E4.justification: v2 Figure 2 introduces an accuracy–diversity frontier and parameter-sensitivity analysis; Appendix B.2 adds runtime and high-temperature failure analysis for eta/epsilon sampling. The original case studies and temperature plots remain. The newly titled AlpacaEval ablation mostly repackages v1 Table 3, while omitting its weaker min-p configurations at temperature 1.5.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without corresponding uncertainty estimates or formal significance tests. v2 Table 4 introduces mean±SD human ratings, and Section 6 reports a paired t-test with p < 0.05. Benchmark seed counts and repeated-run uncertainty remain unspecified.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial baseline, larger-model, accuracy–diversity and human-rating results. For example, Table 3a newly reports Mistral Large GPQA accuracy of 22.77% for min-p versus 2.01% for both top-p settings at temperature 3. Original plots survive in Appendix C.3, but Table 6 omits v1's temperature-1.5 min-p results with win rates 48.13% and 42.09%.

T1.justification: The defining mathematics of min-p remains equivalent, and neither version provides theorems or proofs. v1's background decoding formulas are condensed into prose. v2's threshold example explains the existing rule, while its entropy measure is an evaluation addition without a formal derivation.

C1.justification: The central claim that min-p improves the creativity–coherence balance, especially at high temperatures, is retained. v2 adds an explicit claim of human preference and identifies practical parameter guidelines as a contribution in the introduction.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning scaling to larger models, the accuracy–diversity frontier, parameter sensitivity and practical efficiency relative to eta/epsilon sampling. Appendix A adds specific limitations about hyperparameter selection and evaluating pre-generated rather than interactive outputs, alongside new connections between uncertainty and chain-of-thought reasoning.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands documentation of tested hyperparameters and selection rationale, human-study procedures, A100 runtime observations, and inference-engine integrations. It retains the implementation code and adds an anonymous repository address. However, v1's identification of Claude as the AlpacaEval judge and its explicit Exact Match reporting statement disappear.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning around computationally costly entropy-based methods and connects min-p to risk-based parameter calibration, self-consistency and uncertainty-guided reasoning. It adds relevant work such as Zhou et al. and Wang et al., while dropping v1's dedicated discussions of locally typical sampling and contrastive decoding.

P1.justification: The title and much of the prose are rewritten. Related work moves near the beginning, the separate background section is absorbed into other sections, methodology expands into several subsections, and experiments and results are reorganized. Human evaluation, reproducibility and ethics statements are added, and limitations move to Appendix A.

P2.justification: The main document changes from two columns to one. Figure 1 is rearranged into a grid, the case-study tables are merged, and original benchmark plots move to the appendix. New benchmark summaries, human-rating tables and an accuracy–diversity plot substantially change the presentation. Figure 1's revised caption incorrectly identifies several retained panels.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly identifies its single-model scope and lack of human evaluation as limitations. v2 substantially addresses these through larger-model results and direct human assessments of quality and diversity, reinforced by the new accuracy–diversity analysis and broader baseline comparisons. These additions strengthen evidence for the central claim. The single-prompt human study, omitted weaker AlpacaEval configurations, incomplete experimental details and Figure 1 caption errors qualify—but do not outweigh—the gains.
